title: The law, written down first
plain: A short rule says how many different worlds a set of build orders can make, and the numbers it predicts are saved in the repo before any server run.
why: A prediction made after the answer proves nothing.
done_when: The law's counts match hand values and the predictions file is older than every result.

title: Four experiments against the prediction
plain: Each ticket layout is built on the real server in every order, and the number of different worlds is compared with the prediction.
why: This is where the law can be killed by one wrong number.
done_when: E1 to E4 each have a measured class count and a verdict next to the prediction.

title: How much order the world forgets
plain: The world keeps some facts about how it was built and drops others; we count the dropped information in bits and check that 'same world' behaves like a proper grouping.
why: This is the Godel-style quantity: what a finished world cannot say about its own history.
done_when: The bits lost are computed from measurements and equal the law's value.

title: Has anyone stated this law?
plain: A search of the Minecraft wiki, bug tracker and mathematics papers, with every source and its link kept in one file.
why: A law that already exists in a paper is not a discovery.
done_when: The file lists queries, links, and for each close hit what it does not say.

title: The shape of the real terrain
plain: Real seed 7 terrain is measured with persistent homology: at what price do separate regions join into one.
why: The round 2 map showed only islands; the joining price tells how much digging or swimming a route needs.
done_when: The joining price of start and iron equals an independent cheapest-bottleneck path.

title: Does it change the route?
plain: A planner that may dig through stone and swim at a price is raced against plain breadth-first search with the same number of steps allowed.
why: Round 2 found no route at all on real terrain, so the priced model decides whether routing is possible.
done_when: Equal budgets, a route where round 1 found none, and a stated effect of the build order on the route.

title: Round 3 on the website
plain: A round 3 page shows the goals, their status and each prediction beside its measurement.
why: The owner reads the result on the site, not in the repo.
done_when: site/r3.html loads r3.json and links from the main page.

title: Count worlds by brute force
plain: A small function tries every order of k tickets, treats pairs that cannot swap as fixed, and counts the different results.
why: It gives the law's number without any server.
done_when: Path of 3 gives 4, triangle 6, path of 4 gives 8, four mutually fixed gives 24, no fixed pairs gives 1.

title: A ticket on built ground does nothing
plain: If a ticket's chunk is already built by an earlier ticket it adds nothing, so only the first ticket of a close group matters.
why: This is what turns the 2x2 square's 24 orders into 4.
done_when: The square (all four within 2 chunks) gives 4 classes, one per first ticket.

title: Saved predictions equal the law
plain: The predictions file written by the simulator lane must give the same class counts as the brute-force function for E1, E3 and E4.
why: Two independent routes to the same number.
done_when: E1 4, E3 6, E4 8 in the file; E2 holds a whole number from 1 to 6.

title: Predictions came first
plain: The commit that adds the predictions file must be an ancestor of the commit that adds each experiment result.
why: This is the pre-registration, checked by git itself.
done_when: git says predictions are an ancestor of the E1, E2, E3 and E4 results.

title: E1: a line of 3 tickets 5 apart
plain: All orders of a line of 3 tickets 5 apart are built on the real server; the number of different worlds must equal the prediction (4).
why: Equal numbers support the law; a different number kills it and says which pair of tickets was misjudged.
done_when: Measured classes equal the saved prediction, and the grouping of orders matches too.

title: E2: the 2x2 square seen through the wide window
plain: All orders of the 2x2 square seen through the wide window are built on the real server; the number of different worlds must equal the prediction (5).
why: Equal numbers support the law; a different number kills it and says which pair of tickets was misjudged.
done_when: Measured classes equal the saved prediction, and the grouping of orders matches too.

title: E3: a triangle of 3 tickets 3 apart
plain: All orders of a triangle of 3 tickets 3 apart are built on the real server; the number of different worlds must equal the prediction (6).
why: Equal numbers support the law; a different number kills it and says which pair of tickets was misjudged.
done_when: Measured classes equal the saved prediction, and the grouping of orders matches too.

title: E4: a line of 4 tickets 5 apart
plain: All orders of a line of 4 tickets 5 apart are built on the real server; the number of different worlds must equal the prediction (8).
why: Equal numbers support the law; a different number kills it and says which pair of tickets was misjudged.
done_when: Measured classes equal the saved prediction, and the grouping of orders matches too.

title: Repeat controls are clean
plain: Every experiment repeats at least one order and the two copies must be identical block for block.
why: If a repeat differs, the differences are noise and no class count means anything.
done_when: All repeat controls show 0 differing blocks.

title: Bits lost, by formula
plain: The information lost is log2 of the number of orders divided by the number of worlds; the exact loss counts how many orders share each world.
why: This is the one number the Godel idea needs.
done_when: 24 orders in 4 worlds gives 2.585 bits; 6 orders in 4 worlds gives 0.585.

title: Bits lost, measured
plain: From each experiment's class sizes the bits lost are computed and must equal the value the law predicted.
why: The loss is a prediction too, not just a count.
done_when: Measured bits equal predicted bits for E1 to E4.

title: 'Same world' is a real grouping
plain: If A equals B and B equals C then A must equal C, checked on every measured triple of orders.
why: Without this the classes would not be well defined.
done_when: Zero violating triples in partitions.json.

title: A wider window can only split worlds
plain: Looking at more chunks can separate two worlds that looked equal but never join two that looked different.
why: So 'order does not matter' can be refuted by one block but never proven for every window.
done_when: Classes in the wide window are at least the classes in the narrow window for the same orders.

title: Ore moves in swaps
plain: Between the worlds of the square, iron and gold in chunk (64,64) change by equal and opposite amounts.
why: It shows what the lost information is made of: contested cells, not new material.
done_when: Iron plus gold is 163 in all four classes, diamonds stay 1.

title: Every source has a link and a query
plain: Each entry in the source file has the search words used, a web address and a one-line finding.
why: A claim of 'nobody noticed' must show where we looked.
done_when: Every entry has query, an https address and a finding.

title: The right places were searched
plain: The file covers the Minecraft wiki, the bug tracker, trace monoids, acyclic orientations, left regular bands and order-independent generation.
why: A missing family is a hole in the novelty claim.
done_when: All six families appear with at least one address each.

title: Closest prior work says what it lacks
plain: For each near hit the file states in one line what the law adds that the source does not say.
why: This is the honest edge of the novelty.
done_when: Every near hit has a non-empty 'lacks' line.

title: Persistence output is consistent
plain: At each price level the Euler number from the counts of cells equals components minus loops in the saved output.
why: A wrong persistence run would poison the route model.
done_when: All listed levels agree.

title: Joining price is the cheapest bottleneck
plain: The price at which the start region joins the iron region equals the cheapest path where the dearest step is as small as possible.
why: A known theorem ties persistence to routing; we check it on real terrain.
done_when: The persistence value equals an independent bottleneck search on the seed 7 grid.

title: Dig and swim prices
plain: A prototype lets a route dig through stone or swim water at a set price per step, on a tiny hand-made map.
why: Round 1 treated stone and water as walls, which made real terrain islands.
done_when: The hand map costs exactly the hand-computed total with one dig and one swim.

title: Route cost never beats the bottleneck
plain: A route's total price is at least its dearest single step, equal when the route is one cell wide.
why: This links the terrain measurement to the planner.
done_when: True on three hand maps.

title: Equal step budget
plain: In every row of the race both solvers are allowed the same number of expanded cells.
why: Otherwise the race is not fair.
done_when: Budget equal in every row.

title: Planner against breadth-first search
plain: At equal budget the planner's route price is never above the breadth-first route price.
why: This is the round 2 race, redone on a model where real terrain has routes.
done_when: In every row planner price <= BFS price, or BFS found none.

title: A route on real terrain
plain: The priced model finds a route from the spawn grid start to iron where round 1 found none from 1,417 starts.
why: The islands finding is either dissolved or confirmed.
done_when: At least one start has a route, with its price and step count recorded.

title: What the build order moves
plain: Across the four worlds of the square the order changes iron and gold in chunk (64,64) by 2 but changes diamonds by 0.
why: So the lever reaches iron, not diamonds, for route purposes.
done_when: Iron spread is 2, diamond spread is 0.

title: Merge the cards with status
plain: A script joins the round 3 cards with each goal's status, a missing goal being pending.
why: One file feeds the page.
done_when: build() returns every card with a status.

title: Numbers read from files
plain: The page numbers come from the result files on disk; a missing file shows 'not run', never 0.
why: A zero would look like a measurement.
done_when: Each missing file maps to 'not run'.

title: The round 3 page
plain: One page function draws a card per goal with title, plain text and status.
why: The owner reads the result here.
done_when: Every card has data-goal, title, plain and status.

title: Prediction beside measurement
plain: For each experiment the page shows the predicted class count and the measured one; colour marks only agree or disagree.
why: The law is judged in public.
done_when: Both numbers and a verdict appear for E1 to E4.

title: Status file
plain: A file maps every round 3 goal id to a status, exported by House after each report.
why: The page cannot show a status the harness has not set.
done_when: Every key is an N3 id and every value is a known status.

title: Link from the main page
plain: The main page gets one link to the round 3 page.
why: One door between the pages.
done_when: index.html contains a link to r3.html.

title: Count the corners of a shape
plain: The number of different worlds is also the number of corners of a certain many-sided shape (a hypergraphic polytope) built from the ticket layout; that count is compared with every measured class count.
why: If the corners match the measurements for all layouts, the law is a known geometric object seen in a new place.
done_when: Corner counts equal the measured classes for E1 to E4.
